title: The Bees That Dance
standard_text:
Standard: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A honeybee that finds a patch of flowers comes home with more than nectar. She carries a map. Back inside the dark hive, she climbs onto the honeycomb and begins to move in a pattern her sisters can feel through the wax.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The pattern is called a waggle dance. The bee runs forward in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, loops back, and runs the same line again. Other workers crowd around her and press their antennae against her body.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The straight run carries the message. Its direction, measured against straight up on the vertical comb, tells the other bees the angle to fly relative to the sun. A run pointed straight up means fly toward the sun.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The length of the run tells distance. A longer waggle means a longer flight. A run lasting one second sends the hive roughly a kilometer from home, and the bees adjust for wind without being told.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Karl von Frisch spent decades watching marked bees through glass walls before he worked out what the dance meant. In 1973 he shared a Nobel Prize for it. Many scientists had assumed insects were too simple to pass along anything so exact.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The dance is not perfect. Bees make small errors, and the hive sends out scouts in slightly different directions as a result. Researchers now think the error is useful, because it spreads the search instead of crowding every forager onto one patch.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A honeybee finds a patch of flowers. She comes home with nectar. She also brings a map. Inside the dark hive she climbs onto the honeycomb and starts to move.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The move is called a waggle dance. The bee runs forward in a straight line. She shakes her body side to side. Then she loops back and runs the line again.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The straight run holds the message. Its direction tells the other bees which way to fly. A run that points straight up means fly toward the sun.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The length of the run tells how far. A longer waggle means a longer flight. One second of waggle means about one kilometer.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Karl von Frisch watched bees through glass walls for years. He worked out what the dance meant. He won a Nobel Prize in 1973.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The dance is not perfect. Bees make small errors. That may help them. The errors spread the search over more flowers.

questions.q: What two things does the waggle dance tell the other bees?
questions.a: The direction of the straight run tells them the angle to fly relative to the sun, and the length of the run tells them how far away the flowers are.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. direction) and paragraph D (i.e. distance).
Summarize how a honeybee tells the hive where she found flowers.
questions.a: She dances on the honeycomb, running in a straight line while waggling. The direction of the run gives the angle to the sun and its length gives the distance, so other workers can fly to the same patch.

questions.q:
waggle dance: the pattern a bee runs on the comb to tell other bees where flowers are.
forager: a bee that leaves the hive to collect nectar.
Describe the connection between the small errors in the dance and the hive's search for food.
questions.a: Because bees make small errors, scouts leave in slightly different directions, which spreads the search over more flowers instead of crowding every forager onto one patch.

note: Students may quote any accurate detail, i.e. "a run lasting one second sends the hive roughly a kilometer from home." Check that the quote is copied exactly, which is what RI.5.1 asks for.

title: The Pony Express
standard_text:
Standard: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: In April of 1860, a mail company promised something that sounded impossible. A letter would cross from Missouri to California in ten days. At the time, the fastest mail went by ship around South America and took close to a month.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The plan was a relay of riders. Stations stood roughly ten miles apart along a 1,900-mile trail. A rider galloped in, threw a leather mochila of mail over a fresh horse, and was gone again in two minutes.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Riders were chosen for being light. One advertisement asked for young, skinny, wiry fellows and added that orphans were preferred. Each man carried about twenty pounds of mail and almost nothing else, because weight slowed the horse.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The route crossed the Sierra Nevada in winter and the Great Basin in summer. Riders went through snowdrifts, dust storms, and territory where war had broken out between settlers and the Paiute. Some stations were burned before a rider reached them.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It worked. Lincoln's inaugural address reached Sacramento in seven days and seventeen hours, the fastest the country had ever moved news that far.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The company still failed. The telegraph line reached California in October of 1861, and a message that took ten days by horse took seconds by wire. The Pony Express shut down two days later, after eighteen months.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In April of 1860, a mail company made a promise. A letter would cross from Missouri to California in ten days. Before that, mail went by ship and took a month.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The plan was a relay of riders. Stations stood about ten miles apart. A rider rode in, threw his mail bag onto a fresh horse, and left in two minutes.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Riders had to be light. One ad asked for young, skinny, wiry men. Each rider carried about twenty pounds of mail and little else.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The trail was hard. Riders crossed deep snow in the mountains and dust in the desert. Some stations were burned before a rider got there.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It worked. Lincoln's speech reached Sacramento in seven days and seventeen hours. No news had ever moved that fast.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The company still failed. The telegraph reached California in 1861. A message took seconds by wire. The Pony Express closed two days later.

questions.q: Why did the Pony Express shut down?
questions.a: The telegraph line reached California in October of 1861, and a message that took ten days by horse took seconds by wire, so the company closed two days later.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the relay) and paragraph F (i.e. the telegraph).
Summarize what the Pony Express was and how long it lasted.
questions.a: It was a relay of riders carrying mail 1,900 miles from Missouri to California in about ten days. Stations stood ten miles apart and riders changed horses in two minutes. It ran for eighteen months and closed when the telegraph arrived.

questions.q:
relay: a system in which each rider carries something part of the way and hands it on.
mochila: the leather mail bag a rider threw over a fresh horse.
Describe the connection between the weight a rider carried and the choice of riders.
questions.a: Weight slowed the horse, so the company wanted light riders and asked for young, skinny, wiry fellows who carried about twenty pounds of mail and almost nothing else.

note: The eighteen months are worth drawing out: the Pony Express is remembered far better than it worked, and the text says plainly that the company failed.

title: What a Leaf Loses in Autumn
standard_text:
Standard: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A maple leaf in July is not simply green. It already holds yellow and orange pigments, but the green of chlorophyll is so strong in summer that nothing else shows through.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Chlorophyll is the chemical a leaf uses to turn sunlight into sugar. A tree rebuilds it constantly through the growing season, because sunlight breaks it down almost as fast as the leaf can make it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: As nights lengthen in autumn, the tree stops the rebuilding. A thin layer of cells forms where the leaf stalk meets the branch and begins to seal the connection. Water and nutrients no longer move freely in or out.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The green fades first, because nothing is replacing it. The yellow and orange pigments that were there all along are left behind, and the leaf appears to change color when in fact it is only losing one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Red is different. Many trees make red pigments in autumn, using sugar trapped in the dying leaf. Bright, cool days produce the deepest reds, which is why one autumn is spectacular and the next is dull.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Finally the sealing layer finishes its work. The leaf falls, and the tree keeps the nutrients it pulled back from it. The color a person drives out to see is the last stage of the tree reclaiming what it can.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A maple leaf in July is not only green. It already holds yellow and orange. The green of chlorophyll is so strong that nothing else shows.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Chlorophyll turns sunlight into sugar. A tree makes it all summer long. Sunlight breaks it down almost as fast as the leaf can build it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: In autumn the nights get longer. The tree stops rebuilding chlorophyll. A thin layer of cells seals the leaf stalk to the branch.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The green fades first. Nothing replaces it. The yellow and orange were there all along. The leaf is not gaining a color. It is losing one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Red is different. Many trees make red pigments in autumn from sugar in the leaf. Bright, cool days make the deepest reds.

paras.label: F
paras.text: At last the leaf falls. The tree keeps the nutrients it pulled back. The colors are the last stage of that work.

questions.q: Why does a leaf look green in summer even though yellow pigments are present?
questions.a: The green of chlorophyll is so strong in summer that nothing else shows through, because the tree rebuilds chlorophyll constantly through the growing season.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. losing green) and paragraph E (i.e. making red).
Summarize why leaves change color in autumn.
questions.a: As nights lengthen, the tree stops rebuilding chlorophyll and seals the leaf stalk. The green fades and the yellow and orange that were there all along show. Some trees also make red pigments from sugar trapped in the leaf.

questions.q:
chlorophyll: the green chemical a leaf uses to turn sunlight into sugar.
pigment: a substance that gives something its color.
Describe the connection between the sealing layer and the color of the leaf.
questions.a: The sealing layer stops water and nutrients from moving, so chlorophyll is no longer replaced and the green fades, which lets the yellow and orange show and traps the sugar used to make red.

note: The common answer is that leaves turn yellow. The text says the opposite for yellow and orange: those were already there, and the leaf loses green. Red is the one that is genuinely made in autumn.

title: Ellis Island
standard_text:
Standard: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Between 1892 and 1954, about twelve million people entered the United States through a building on a small island in New York Harbor. Most of them had spent one to two weeks at sea to get there.

paras.label: B
paras.text: First and second class passengers were inspected on the ship and usually walked straight off onto the pier. Everyone in steerage, the cheapest section below deck, was ferried to Ellis Island instead.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The first test came before anyone spoke. Doctors watched arrivals climb a flight of stairs carrying their luggage, looking for anyone short of breath or limping. That climb was called the six-second physical.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Inspectors in the Great Hall asked a list of twenty-nine questions: name, trade, destination, how much money a person carried. The questions were meant to find out whether an arrival could support themselves.

paras.label: E
paras.text: About two in every hundred were sent back. The most common reasons were contagious disease and a judgment that a person was likely to need public support. Families were sometimes separated by that decision.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The island is a museum now. Its records are searchable, and many Americans can find the exact line where an ancestor's name, age and trade were written down by an inspector.

paras.label: A
paras.text: From 1892 to 1954, about twelve million people came into the United States through Ellis Island. It sat on a small island in New York Harbor. Most had been at sea for one or two weeks.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Rich passengers were checked on the ship. They walked straight off onto the pier. People in the cheapest part of the ship were taken to Ellis Island.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The first test came before anyone spoke. Doctors watched people climb the stairs with their bags. They looked for anyone short of breath.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Inspectors asked twenty-nine questions. They asked for a name, a trade, and a destination. They asked how much money a person had.

paras.label: E
paras.text: About two in every hundred were sent back. The usual reasons were illness or no way to earn a living. Some families were split up.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The island is a museum now. The records can be searched. Many Americans can find an ancestor's name on a page.

questions.q: Why were first and second class passengers treated differently from people in steerage?
questions.a: First and second class passengers were inspected on the ship and walked straight off onto the pier, while everyone in steerage was ferried to Ellis Island to be inspected there.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the stairs) and paragraph D (i.e. the questions).
Summarize what happened to an arrival at Ellis Island.
questions.a: A person in steerage was ferried to the island, watched by doctors while climbing the stairs, and then asked twenty-nine questions in the Great Hall about name, trade and money. About two in every hundred were sent back.

questions.q:
steerage: the cheapest section of a ship, below deck.
contagious: able to spread from one person to another.
Describe the connection between the stairs and the doctors' work.
questions.a: Doctors watched arrivals climb the stairs carrying luggage so they could spot anyone short of breath or limping, which is why the climb was called the six-second physical.

note: Two in every hundred is worth putting on the board as a fraction. Students often picture Ellis Island as a place that turned people away, and the text says ninety-eight of every hundred went through.

title: How a Volcano Builds an Island
standard_text:
Standard: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Hawaiian Islands sit in the middle of a tectonic plate, far from the edges where most volcanoes form. The reason is a hot spot: a column of unusually hot rock rising from deep inside the Earth.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The hot spot stays roughly in place. The Pacific Plate above it does not, drifting northwest at about the speed a fingernail grows, four inches a year.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Where the plate passes over the hot spot, magma burns through and erupts onto the seafloor. Cold water chills the lava instantly, and it piles up in rounded lobes called pillow lava, layer on layer.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Building an island this way takes hundreds of thousands of years. The pile must rise through three miles of ocean before any part of it breaks the surface and becomes land.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then the plate carries the new island away from its source. Cut off from the magma, the volcano goes quiet, and waves and rain begin to wear it down faster than it can grow.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The whole chain records the process. Kauai, in the northwest, is old and deeply carved by valleys. The Big Island, still over the hot spot, is erupting. Southeast of it, a seamount is building toward the surface.

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Hawaiian Islands sit in the middle of a plate. Most volcanoes form at the edges. These islands form over a hot spot. That is a column of hot rock from deep inside the Earth.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The hot spot stays in one place. The plate above it moves. It drifts northwest about four inches a year.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Magma burns through the plate and erupts on the seafloor. Cold water chills the lava fast. It piles up in rounded lobes called pillow lava.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Building an island takes a very long time. The pile has to rise through three miles of ocean. Only then does it become land.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then the plate carries the island away. The volcano goes quiet. Waves and rain wear it down.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The chain shows each step. Kauai is old and carved by valleys. The Big Island still erupts. A new seamount is rising to the southeast.

questions.q: Why are the Hawaiian Islands in the middle of a plate instead of at its edge?
questions.a: They form over a hot spot, a column of unusually hot rock rising from deep inside the Earth, rather than at the plate edges where most volcanoes form.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the moving plate) and paragraph F (i.e. the chain).
Summarize how the hot spot builds a chain of islands.
questions.a: Magma from the hot spot erupts onto the seafloor and piles up until it breaks the surface. The plate then carries that island away, the volcano goes quiet, and a new one begins over the hot spot.

questions.q:
hot spot: a column of unusually hot rock rising from deep inside the Earth.
seamount: an underwater mountain that has not yet reached the surface.
Describe the connection between the moving plate and the ages of the islands.
questions.a: Because the plate drifts northwest while the hot spot stays in place, islands made earlier are carried away and worn down, so Kauai in the northwest is old while the Big Island is still erupting.

note: Four inches a year is a useful number to compare with the age of the chain. Ask what else the class knows that moves at the speed a fingernail grows.

title: The Erie Canal
standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more main ideas of a text and explain how they are supported by key details; summarize the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1817, New York began digging a ditch four feet deep and forty feet wide across the width of the state. Critics in Washington called it Clinton's Ditch, after the governor who pushed it, and refused to pay for any of it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The problem it solved was cost. Moving a ton of flour from Buffalo to New York City by wagon took three weeks and cost about a hundred dollars. The same ton by canal boat would cost less than ten.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Nobody in the country had built anything like it. The engineers were surveyors and lawyers who learned on the job, inventing a stump puller and a cement that would harden underwater because they could not buy either one.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The land itself was the obstacle. Lake Erie sits almost six hundred feet above the Hudson River, so the canal needed eighty-three locks, each one a chamber that raised or lowered a boat like a step.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It opened in 1825, eight years after the first shovel. Freight costs fell by ninety per cent, and towns strung along the route grew faster than almost anywhere else in the country.

paras.label: F
paras.text: New York City was the biggest winner. The canal made it the cheapest door to the whole interior of the continent, and within fifteen years it handled more trade than Boston, Baltimore and Philadelphia together.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1817, New York began digging a ditch across the whole state. It was four feet deep and forty feet wide. Critics called it Clinton's Ditch. Washington would not pay for it.

paras.label: B

paras.label: C

paras.label: D

paras.label: E

paras.text: New York City won the most. The canal made it the cheapest door to the interior. Soon it handled more trade than three other big ports together.

questions.q: Name two main ideas of this article and one detail that supports each.
questions.a: One main idea is that the canal cut the cost of moving freight, supported by the ton of flour falling from about a hundred dollars to less than ten. Another is that the canal made New York City the country's busiest port, supported by its handling more trade than Boston, Baltimore and Philadelphia together.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the cost) and paragraph D (i.e. the locks).
Summarize the Erie Canal in three sentences.
questions.a: New York dug a canal across the state between 1817 and 1825. It needed eighty-three locks to climb almost six hundred feet from the Hudson River to Lake Erie. Freight costs fell by ninety per cent and New York City became the cheapest door to the interior.

questions.q:
lock: a chamber on a canal that raises or lowers a boat like a step.
freight: goods carried from one place to another.
Describe the connection between the eighty-three locks and the height of Lake Erie.
questions.a: Lake Erie sits almost six hundred feet above the Hudson River, so the canal needed eighty-three locks to raise and lower boats that whole distance in steps.

note: RI.5.2 asks for two or more main ideas. Accept any two the text supports, i.e. cost, engineering learned on the job, or the rise of New York City, so long as the student names a detail for each.

title: The Owl's Silent Wing
standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more main ideas of a text and explain how they are supported by key details; summarize the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A pigeon taking off from a branch can be heard across a yard. A barn owl crossing the same yard is nearly silent, and the difference is in the feathers rather than the bird's care.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Noise in flight comes from turbulence. Air rolling off the sharp back edge of a wing breaks into swirls, and those swirls make the rushing sound a person hears when a bird passes overhead.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The leading edge of an owl's wing is not smooth. It carries a comb of stiff bristles that splits the oncoming air into smaller streams before it can build into one large, noisy swirl.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The back edge is frayed rather than sharp. It ends in a soft fringe that lets the separated streams rejoin gradually, and the wing surface itself is covered in a velvety down that absorbs the high notes.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The quiet costs the owl something. The same soft feathers soak up water, so owls hunt poorly in heavy rain, and the structures only work at the slow speeds an owl flies.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Engineers have copied the design. Serrated edges based on owl feathers now appear on wind turbine blades and aircraft landing gear, where they cut noise without changing how the surface carries a load.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A pigeon taking off can be heard across a yard. A barn owl is nearly silent. The difference is in its feathers, not in how carefully it flies.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Noise in flight comes from turbulence. Air rolls off the back edge of a wing. It breaks into swirls. Those swirls make the rushing sound.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The front edge of an owl's wing is not smooth. It has a comb of stiff bristles. The comb splits the air into smaller streams.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The back edge is frayed, not sharp. A soft fringe lets the streams join again slowly. The wing is also covered in velvety down.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The quiet costs the owl something. The soft feathers soak up water. Owls hunt poorly in heavy rain.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Engineers have copied the design. Wind turbine blades now use serrated edges like owl feathers. They cut the noise.

questions.q: Name two main ideas of this article and one detail that supports each.
questions.a: One main idea is that feathers rather than care make an owl quiet, supported by the comb of stiff bristles on the leading edge. Another is that the quiet has a cost, supported by the soft feathers soaking up water so owls hunt poorly in heavy rain.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the leading edge) and paragraph D (i.e. the back edge).
Summarize how an owl flies silently.
questions.a: A comb of stiff bristles on the leading edge splits the oncoming air into smaller streams, a soft fringe at the back lets them rejoin gradually, and velvety down absorbs the high notes, so no large noisy swirl ever forms.

questions.q:
turbulence: air breaking into swirls as it rolls off a wing.
serrated: having a row of small teeth or notches along an edge.
Describe the connection between the owl's feathers and the design of wind turbine blades.
questions.a: Engineers copied the serrated edges of owl feathers onto turbine blades because the same structure cuts noise without changing how the surface carries a load.

note: Paragraph E is the one students skip. A good second main idea has to account for the cost of the quiet, not only the cleverness of it.

title: The Boys Who Planted a Forest
standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more main ideas of a text and explain how they are supported by key details; summarize the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1933, a quarter of American workers had no job. One of the first programs of the new administration put young men to work outdoors, in a corps that would last nine years and enroll about three million of them.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The deal was plain. A man between eighteen and twenty-five signed up for six months, lived in a camp, and earned thirty dollars a month. Twenty-five of those dollars were sent home to his family.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The work was the kind no company would pay for. Crews built trails, fought fires, strung telephone line, and cut the roads and shelters that turned raw land into usable state parks.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Above all they planted trees. The corps put roughly three billion seedlings into the ground, more than half of all the trees planted in the United States up to that time.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The camps taught as well as worked. Many enrollees arrived unable to read, and evening classes in the camps taught more than forty thousand men to do so before they went home.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The corps was not open to everyone equally. Camps were segregated by race after 1935, and women were excluded entirely, which belongs in the record alongside the trails and the trees.

paras.text: In 1933, a quarter of American workers had no job. A new program put young men to work outdoors. It lasted nine years. About three million men joined.

questions.a: One main idea is that the corps gave jobless young men work and pay, supported by the thirty dollars a month with twenty-five sent home. Another is that the work changed the land, supported by the roughly three billion seedlings the corps planted.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the trees) and paragraph F (i.e. who was left out).
Summarize what the corps was and what it did.
questions.a: From 1933 it enrolled about three million young men for six months at a time, paying thirty dollars a month with twenty-five sent home. They built trails, fought fires and planted roughly three billion seedlings, and evening classes taught more than forty thousand of them to read.

questions.q:
corps: an organized body of people working together under one command.
segregated: kept apart by race.
Describe the connection between the pay a man earned and his family at home.
questions.a: A man earned thirty dollars a month and twenty-five of those dollars were sent home, so his family was supported by work he did in a camp far away.

note: Paragraph F is deliberately not a footnote. A summary that leaves out the segregated camps has left out a main idea, not a detail.

title: The Tide and the Moon
standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more main ideas of a text and explain how they are supported by key details; summarize the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Twice a day most coasts rise and fall by several feet. The cause is gravity, but not quite in the way most explanations suggest, because there are two bulges of water and only one moon.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The moon pulls hardest on the water nearest it, raising a bulge on that side of the Earth. It also pulls the solid Earth away from the water on the far side, which leaves a second bulge behind.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The Earth turns underneath those bulges. A given beach passes through both of them in a day, which is why most places get two high tides and two low tides in about twenty-five hours.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The sun pulls too, with less than half the effect. When sun and moon line up, the bulges add together into the large spring tides; when they sit at right angles, the smaller neap tides result.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Shape matters as much as gravity. In the open ocean the bulge is barely three feet high, but a funnel-shaped bay can squeeze it upward, and the Bay of Fundy regularly sees a range above fifty feet.

paras.label: F
paras.text: All that water moving twice a day carries energy. Tidal power stations in France and South Korea run turbines on the flow, and unlike wind or sun, the schedule is known for centuries ahead.

questions.q: Name two main ideas of this article and one detail that supports each.
questions.a: One main idea is that the moon raises two bulges rather than one, supported by its pulling the solid Earth away from the water on the far side. Another is that the shape of a coast decides the size of a tide, supported by the Bay of Fundy's range above fifty feet.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. two bulges) and paragraph E (i.e. the shape of a bay).
Summarize what causes the tides.
questions.a: The moon raises a bulge of water on the near side of the Earth and leaves a second on the far side. The Earth turns through both, giving most coasts two high tides a day, and the sun and the shape of a bay make them larger or smaller.

questions.q:
bulge: a swelling of water raised by gravity.
range: the distance between high tide and low tide.
Describe the connection between the position of the sun and the size of a tide.
questions.a: When the sun and moon line up their pulls add together and the tides are large, and when they sit at right angles the tides are small.

note: The second bulge is the part worth slowing down for. Most students will say the moon pulls the water up, which explains one high tide a day, not two.

title: The Silk Road
standard_text:
Standard: Determine two or more main ideas of a text and explain how they are supported by key details; summarize the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Silk Road was never a road, and silk was only part of what moved along it. The name describes a web of routes that linked China to the Mediterranean for roughly fifteen hundred years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Almost nobody travelled the whole distance. Goods changed hands at market after market, so a bolt of silk that began near Xi'an might pass through a dozen owners before a Roman bought it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Each exchange raised the price. Silk in Rome cost many times what it cost in China, and Roman writers complained about the silver leaving the empire to pay for cloth.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Ideas travelled in the same packs. Paper making moved west from China, Buddhism moved east into China, and both arrived with traders rather than with armies.

paras.label: E
paras.text: So did disease. The plague that struck Europe in the fourteenth century is thought to have followed trade routes west, carried by fleas on rats in the holds and packs of merchants.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The routes faded when ships got better. Once Portuguese and later Dutch vessels could carry a cargo from Asia to Europe by sea, the overland journey cost more than it was worth.

overland: across land rather than by sea.
bolt: a long roll of cloth as it is sold.
Describe the connection between the number of times goods changed hands and the price of silk in Rome.

note: The title is the lesson. Ask what the class pictured before reading paragraph A, and what the text says instead.

title: The Beaver and the Flood
standard_text:
Standard: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text based on specific information in the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A beaver does not set out to build a wetland. It is responding to a sound. Running water triggers an urge to pile sticks and mud against it, and the beaver keeps piling until the sound stops.

paras.label: B
paras.text: What the animal makes, almost by accident, is a pond. Water backs up behind the dam, spreads sideways across flat ground, and soaks into soil that a fast stream would have carried past.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That stored water changes the stream below. In a heavy rain the pond holds part of the surge and lets it out slowly, so the flood peak downstream arrives lower and later than it otherwise would.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The same pond helps in the opposite weather. Water that soaked into the banks seeps back out through the dry months, keeping a trickle in channels that would run dry without it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Other species follow the water. Dead standing trees in the flooded ground become nest holes for woodpeckers and ducks, and the slow water suits frogs, dragonflies and young fish far better than the old stream did.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Trappers removed most North American beavers by the middle of the nineteenth century, and the streams changed with them. Several states now move beavers back on purpose, as cheaper flood control than anything a crew can build.

questions.q: What makes a beaver begin building a dam?
questions.a: The sound of running water triggers an urge to pile sticks and mud against it, and the beaver keeps piling until the sound stops.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. floods) and paragraph D (i.e. dry months).
Summarize how one beaver dam changes a stream.
questions.a: The dam backs water up into a pond that soaks into the ground. In heavy rain the pond holds part of the surge so the flood downstream is lower and later, and in dry months the stored water seeps back out to keep a trickle running.

questions.q:
surge: a sudden rush of water.
channel: the bed a stream runs along.
Describe the connection between the beaver's dam and the birds that nest nearby.
questions.a: The dam floods the ground and kills standing trees, and those dead trees become nest holes for woodpeckers and ducks.

note: RI.5.3 wants the interaction named, not just the two things. Push for because and so: the dam stores water, so the flood peak arrives lower and later.

title: The Interpreter on the Expedition
standard_text:
Standard: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text based on specific information in the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: When Lewis and Clark set out up the Missouri River in 1804, they could speak none of the languages of the nations whose land they were crossing. Every conversation would have to pass through somebody.

paras.label: B
paras.text: At a Mandan village that winter they hired a French Canadian trader named Charbonneau. The reason was his wife. Sacagawea was Lemhi Shoshone, taken from her people as a child, and the expedition would need the Shoshone.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The need was horses. To cross the Rocky Mountains the party had to leave the river and buy pack animals, and the Shoshone had them. Without horses the expedition would have stopped at the mountains.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Communication ran through a chain. Sacagawea spoke Shoshone to a captured Shoshone speaker, who spoke Hidatsa to Charbonneau, who spoke French to a soldier, who spoke English to the captains. One question could take several minutes.

paras.label: E
paras.text: When the party finally met a Shoshone band in August of 1805, the chief turned out to be Sacagawea's brother. The expedition got its horses and a guide over the pass.

paras.label: F
paras.text: She did more than translate. A travelling party that included a woman and an infant read as a peaceful one, and Clark wrote in his journal that her presence reassured every group they met.

questions.q: Why did the expedition need to reach the Shoshone?
questions.a: To cross the Rocky Mountains the party had to leave the river and buy pack animals, and the Shoshone had the horses they needed.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the horses) and paragraph D (i.e. the chain of languages).
Summarize Sacagawea's part in the expedition.
questions.a: She was hired with her husband because she spoke Shoshone, and the party needed Shoshone horses to cross the Rocky Mountains. She translated through a chain of four languages, the Shoshone chief turned out to be her brother, and her presence made the party look peaceful.

questions.q:
interpreter: a person who turns speech from one language into another.
expedition: a journey made by a group with a set purpose.
Describe the connection between Sacagawea's childhood and the success of the expedition.
questions.a: She had been taken from the Lemhi Shoshone as a child, so she could speak Shoshone, and when the party met a Shoshone band the chief turned out to be her brother, which is how they got their horses.

note: The chain in paragraph D is worth acting out with four students. It makes the point that the expedition's survival ran through one person's childhood language.

title: The Fig and the Wasp
standard_text:
Standard: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text based on specific information in the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A fig is not a fruit in the ordinary sense. It is a hollow ball lined on the inside with hundreds of tiny flowers, all of them facing inward where no bee can reach them.

paras.label: B
paras.text: One insect can get in. A female fig wasp, about the size of a grain of rice, pushes through a narrow opening at the end of the fig, usually tearing off her wings and antennae on the way.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Inside, she lays eggs in some flowers and leaves pollen on others. The pollinated flowers become seeds; the ones holding eggs become galls, small chambers where wasp larvae grow. Then she dies inside the fig.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The next generation mates in the dark. Wingless males chew exits through the fig wall and die; the winged females collect pollen, crawl out through those tunnels, and fly off to find another tree.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Neither species can manage alone. A fig tree without its wasp sets no seed, and a wasp without a fig has nowhere to lay eggs, so each depends on the other for its next generation.

paras.label: F
paras.text: There are more than seven hundred fig species, and most are pollinated by a wasp species found in no other fig. That pairing is one of the tightest partnerships known in nature.

questions.q: Why can a bee not pollinate a fig?
questions.a: The flowers are inside a hollow ball and all face inward, so no bee can reach them and only a wasp small enough to push through the narrow opening can get in.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. what she does inside) and paragraph E (i.e. why neither can manage alone).
Summarize how a fig and its wasp depend on each other.
questions.a: A female wasp pushes into the hollow fig, lays eggs in some flowers and leaves pollen on others, then dies inside. Her young mate in the dark and the females carry pollen to another tree, so the fig gets its seeds and the wasp gets somewhere to lay eggs.

questions.q:
pollen: the dust a flower needs from another flower in order to make seed.
gall: a small chamber in a plant where an insect larva grows.
Describe the connection between the number of fig species and the number of wasp species.
questions.a: There are more than seven hundred fig species and most are pollinated by a wasp found in no other fig, so the two groups have paired off almost one for one.

note: Students usually ask whether they are eating wasps. The text says she dies inside, and the fig digests her; that is worth answering plainly rather than dodging.

title: The Telegraph and the Railroad
standard_text:
Standard: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text based on specific information in the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two inventions arrived in America within a few years of each other, and neither one worked well until it was paired with the other. One moved goods; the other moved words.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Early railroads ran on single tracks. Two trains headed toward each other on the same rail had no way to know it, and the schedule printed on paper was the only thing keeping them apart.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Collisions were common enough to have a name. A head-on crash was called a cornfield meet, and in 1851 a superintendent on the Erie Railroad used a telegraph line to hold one train while another passed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That order was the beginning of dispatching. From then on a man at a desk could know where every train on a line actually was, not where a printed timetable said it ought to be.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The railroad returned the favor. Telegraph companies strung their wire along the cleared, fenced, patrolled strip of land a railroad already owned, which was the cheapest right of way in the country.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The two spread together across the continent. Where the rails went, the wire went beside them, and a town that got one almost always got the other in the same year.

note: This is a two-way relationship, which is harder than cause and effect. Ask for one sentence in each direction before accepting an answer.

title: Why the Sahara Feeds the Amazon
standard_text:
Standard: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text based on specific information in the text.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Amazon rainforest grows on soil that is surprisingly poor. Heavy rain washes nutrients down past the roots year after year, and phosphorus in particular drains away faster than the forest can replace it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Some of the replacement comes from four thousand miles away. Every year winds lift dust from the Sahara and carry it west across the Atlantic in a haze that satellites can follow from space.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Most of that dust starts in one place. The Bodele Depression in Chad is the dried bed of an ancient lake, and the sediment there is packed with the remains of freshwater organisms rich in phosphorus.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Satellite measurements put the delivery at roughly twenty-eight million tons of dust a year, of which about twenty-two thousand tons is phosphorus, close to what the rain strips out of the soil.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The link runs on the seasons. The dust blows in winter, when the trade winds are strongest and the Sahara is driest, and much of it falls out over the basin in the rains that follow.

paras.label: F
paras.text: It is a reminder that the parts of the Earth are not separate. A dry lake bed in Chad helps keep the largest rainforest on the planet in leaf.

phosphorus: a nutrient plants need in order to grow.

note: Pair this with a globe. The distance is the part that makes the relationship memorable, and students should trace the route before they explain it.

title: The Words on a Dollar Bill
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 5 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A dollar bill is covered in words, and most of them are doing legal work rather than decoration. Reading them carefully is a short lesson in what money actually is.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Across the top it says Federal Reserve Note. A note is a promise to pay, and the Federal Reserve is the central bank that issues it. The bill is a claim, not a piece of valuable material.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Below the portrait runs a line saying the note is legal tender for all debts, public and private. Legal tender means a creditor must accept it to settle a debt. It does not mean a shop must accept it for a sandwich.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Two signatures appear, the Treasurer of the United States and the Secretary of the Treasury. Their presence marks the note as officially issued, in the way a signature marks a check.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The Latin motto E pluribus unum means out of many, one. Annuit coeptis, printed above the pyramid on the back, is usually translated as he approves of our undertakings.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Older bills said something different. Before 1964 a silver certificate promised to pay the bearer one silver dollar on demand. The promise was dropped, and the words on the bill changed with it.

note: Hand out a real bill if you can. RI.5.4 is about meaning in context, and the context here is an object every student has handled without reading.

title: Naming the Clouds
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 5 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Before 1802 clouds had no shared names. A farmer and a sailor might describe the same sky in completely different words, and no two accounts of the weather could be compared with each other.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A London chemist named Luke Howard proposed a system built out of Latin pieces. Cumulus means heap, stratus means layer, cirrus means curl, and nimbus means rain.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The pieces combine. A cumulonimbus is a heap cloud that is raining, and the name carries both facts in one word without any need for a picture.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Height is added in front. Alto marks the middle level of the sky, so altostratus is a layer cloud at middle height, while plain stratus sits low.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The power of the system is that it describes rather than labels. A person who knows four roots can look at a cloud they have never seen before and say roughly what it is and what it is doing.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Howard's names were adopted internationally and are still in use more than two centuries later. The World Meteorological Organization now recognizes ten main types, all of them built from his original pieces.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Before 1802 clouds had no shared names. A farmer and a sailor might describe the same sky in different words. No two reports could be compared.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Luke Howard was a London chemist. He built a system out of Latin pieces. Cumulus means heap. Stratus means layer. Cirrus means curl. Nimbus means rain.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The pieces combine. A cumulonimbus is a heap cloud that is raining. The name holds both facts in one word.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Height is added in front. Alto marks the middle of the sky. Altostratus is a layer cloud at middle height. Plain stratus sits low.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The system describes instead of labels. Learn four roots and you can read a cloud you have never seen.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Howard's names spread around the world. They are still used today. Ten main types are built from his pieces.

questions.q: What does the name cumulonimbus tell you about a cloud?
questions.a: Cumulus means heap and nimbus means rain, so a cumulonimbus is a heap cloud that is raining.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the Latin roots) and paragraph D (i.e. height).
Summarize the system Luke Howard invented.
questions.a: He named clouds from Latin roots: cumulus for heap, stratus for layer, cirrus for curl and nimbus for rain, with alto in front for middle height. The pieces combine, so a name describes what a cloud is and what it is doing.

questions.q:
root: a word part that carries meaning and combines with others.
cirrus: a curl of cloud high in the sky.
Describe the connection between knowing the Latin roots and reading a new cloud.
questions.a: Because each root describes a shape or a behavior, a person who knows four of them can look at a cloud they have never seen and say roughly what it is and what it is doing.

note: Build the words on the board from the pieces rather than giving them whole. The point of RI.5.4 here is that a reader can take a long word apart.

title: What a Map's Legend Tells You
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 5 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A map is a set of agreements. Every line and color on it stands for something, and the box that spells out those agreements is called the legend, or sometimes the key.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The scale is the first agreement to find. A bar scale shows how far a given length on the paper reaches on the ground, so one inch might stand for ten miles or for ten feet.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Symbols carry the rest. A dashed line is usually a trail, a double line a divided highway, a small cross a church or a cemetery, and a dotted blue line a stream that runs only part of the year.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Color is a shorthand too. On a topographic map green means vegetation, blue means water and brown means the contour lines that show the shape of the land.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Contour lines are the hardest part of a legend to read. Each line joins points of equal elevation, so lines crowded together mean a steep slope and lines far apart mean nearly flat ground.

paras.label: F
paras.text: None of these are universal. A symbol that means one thing on a hiking map can mean another on a city plan, which is why every careful reader starts with the legend rather than the picture.

questions.q: What does it mean when contour lines are crowded together?
questions.a: Each contour line joins points of equal elevation, so lines crowded together mean a steep slope and lines far apart mean nearly flat ground.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the scale) and paragraph E (i.e. contour lines).
Summarize what a legend does for a map reader.
questions.a: It states the agreements the map is built on: the scale that turns a length on paper into a distance on the ground, the symbols for trails, highways and streams, and the colors for vegetation, water and the contour lines showing the shape of the land.

questions.q:
legend: the box on a map that explains what its symbols mean.
elevation: how high a point is above sea level.
Describe the connection between the last paragraph and the advice to read the legend first.
questions.a: A symbol that means one thing on a hiking map can mean another on a city plan, so the legend is the only place a reader can learn what this particular map's lines and colors stand for.

note: Two maps of the same place with different legends make this concrete in about four minutes.

title: What a Chance of Rain Really Means
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 5 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A forecast that says a forty per cent chance of rain is one of the most misread sentences in daily life. It does not mean forty per cent of the area, and it does not mean rain for forty per cent of the day.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The number is a probability of precipitation, and it has a definition. It is the chance that measurable rain, meaning at least one hundredth of an inch, falls at any given point in the forecast area.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Forecasters reach it by combining two judgments: how confident they are that rain will form at all, and how much of the area it would cover if it did. A forty per cent chance can come from either one.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The word measurable is doing real work. A drizzle that wets the pavement but never reaches a hundredth of an inch does not count, which is why a day can feel damp and still be recorded as dry.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Forecasts are checked afterward. Over many days carrying a forty per cent forecast, rain should fall on close to forty per cent of them, and forecasters track that record for themselves.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Knowing the definition changes what a person does with it. Forty per cent is not a promise about the sky; it is a statement about how often a day like today turns out wet.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A forty per cent chance of rain is often misread. It does not mean forty per cent of the area. It does not mean rain for forty per cent of the day.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The number is a probability of precipitation. It has a definition. It is the chance that measurable rain falls at any one point in the area.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Forecasters mix two judgments. One is how sure they are that rain will form. One is how much area it would cover. Either can give forty per cent.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The word measurable matters. A drizzle that never reaches a hundredth of an inch does not count. A damp day can still be recorded as dry.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Forecasts get checked later. Over many forty per cent days, rain should fall on about forty of every hundred.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The definition changes how to use it. Forty per cent is not a promise. It says how often a day like today turns out wet.

questions.q: What does a forty per cent chance of rain actually mean?
questions.a: It is the chance that measurable rain, meaning at least one hundredth of an inch, falls at any given point in the forecast area.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the definition) and paragraph D (i.e. the word measurable).
Summarize how a forecaster arrives at a chance of rain.
questions.a: The forecaster combines how confident they are that rain will form with how much of the area it would cover, and the result is the chance that at least a hundredth of an inch falls at any given point.

questions.q:
probability: how likely something is, given as a number.
precipitation: rain, snow or any water falling from the sky.
Describe the connection between the definition of measurable rain and a day that feels damp but counts as dry.
questions.a: Measurable rain means at least one hundredth of an inch, so a drizzle that wets the pavement without reaching that amount does not count and the day is recorded as dry.

note: Collect the class's guesses before reading paragraph A. Most rooms produce all three wrong readings, which makes the definition land.

title: The Vocabulary of an Election
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 5 topic or subject area.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Election coverage runs on a vocabulary that is rarely explained. The words are ordinary enough to slide past a reader, and specific enough that missing one changes the meaning of a whole sentence.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A candidate stands for office; an incumbent is the one who already holds it. The distinction matters because incumbents win far more often than challengers, so the label carries a prediction with it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A primary is an election to choose a party's candidate. A general election is the one held between parties. A voter can take part in both, and the two can produce very different turnout.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Turnout is the share of eligible voters who actually vote. A race decided by a landslide in the count can still be decided by a minority of the people entitled to take part.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A ballot is the list a voter marks, and a ballot measure is a question put directly to voters rather than to a legislature. Several states decide major laws that way.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The word poll does double duty. A polling place is where ballots are cast, while a poll is a survey of what people say they will do, which is a guess rather than a count.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Election news runs on special words. They are ordinary enough to slide past. Missing one can change a whole sentence.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A candidate runs for office. An incumbent already holds it. Incumbents win far more often than challengers.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A primary chooses a party's candidate. A general election is the one between parties. A voter can take part in both.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Turnout is the share of eligible voters who vote. A race won by a landslide can still be decided by a minority of them.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A ballot is the list a voter marks. A ballot measure is a question put straight to voters. Some states decide big laws that way.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The word poll does two jobs. A polling place is where ballots are cast. A poll is a survey of what people say they will do.

questions.q: What is the difference between a primary and a general election?
questions.a: A primary is an election to choose a party's candidate, and a general election is the one held between parties.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. incumbent) and paragraph F (i.e. the two meanings of poll).
Summarize what the words in this article let a reader understand.
questions.a: They separate a candidate from an incumbent, a primary from a general election, and a polling place from a poll. They also name turnout, the share of eligible voters who vote, and a ballot measure, a question put directly to voters.

questions.q:
incumbent: the person who already holds the office.
turnout: the share of eligible voters who actually vote.
Describe the connection between turnout and a landslide result.
questions.a: Turnout is the share of eligible voters who actually vote, so a race decided by a landslide in the count can still be decided by a minority of the people entitled to take part.

note: The two meanings of poll in paragraph F are the ones that cause real confusion in news reports. Ask for a sentence using each.

title: Two Texts: How a Hurricane Forms
standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the overall structure of events, ideas, concepts, or information in two or more texts.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A science museum and a state emergency agency both publish a page about hurricanes. The facts in them barely differ. The order of those facts differs completely, and the order is what each page is for.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The museum page is a chronology. It starts with warm ocean water, moves to rising air and falling pressure, then to the spiral of thunderstorms, and ends with a named storm crossing a coast.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Reading it, a person learns how one stage leads to the next. The question it answers is how does this happen, and it answers it in time order from first to last.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The agency page is problem and solution. It opens with what a storm surge does to a house, then gives the actions a family should take at seventy-two hours, forty-eight hours, and twenty-four hours before landfall.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Reading that one, a person learns what to do. It answers a different question, which is what should I do, and it is organized by how much time is left rather than by how a storm forms.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Neither structure is better. A student writing a report needs the chronology; a family watching a forecast needs the problem and solution. Noticing the structure tells a reader which text will answer their question.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A science museum and a state agency both write about hurricanes. The facts are nearly the same. The order is not. The order is what each page is for.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The museum page is a chronology. It starts with warm ocean water. Then air rises and pressure falls. Then thunderstorms spiral. Then a named storm crosses a coast.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Reading it, a person learns how one stage leads to the next. It answers the question how does this happen.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The agency page is problem and solution. It opens with what a storm surge does to a house. Then it lists what a family should do at seventy-two, forty-eight and twenty-four hours.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Reading that one, a person learns what to do. It is ordered by how much time is left.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Neither structure is better. A student needs the chronology. A family needs the solutions. The structure tells you which text answers your question.

questions.q: How are the two pages the same, and how are they different?
questions.a: The facts in them barely differ, but the order does: the museum page runs in time order from warm ocean water to landfall, and the agency page runs from the problem of storm surge to the actions a family should take.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the chronology) and paragraph D (i.e. problem and solution).
Summarize why the same facts are arranged two different ways.
questions.a: The museum page is a chronology because it answers how a hurricane happens, and the agency page is problem and solution because it answers what a family should do. Each structure serves the question that page exists to answer.

questions.q:
chronology: an account arranged in time order.
landfall: the moment a storm crosses from the sea onto the coast.
Describe the connection between a reader's question and the structure they should choose.
questions.a: A student writing a report needs the chronology that explains how one stage leads to the next, while a family watching a forecast needs the problem and solution page organized by how much time is left.

note: RI.5.5 is about structure, not topic. Ask students to name the structure before they say anything about hurricanes.

title: Two Texts: The Gold Rush
standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the overall structure of events, ideas, concepts, or information in two or more texts.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two accounts of the California gold rush sit side by side in a textbook. One is a timeline; the other is a cause and effect chain. They cover the same eight years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The timeline begins in January of 1848, when gold was found at a sawmill on the American River, and runs forward: the news reaching the east, the ships, the overland crossings, statehood in 1850.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It is easy to follow and easy to quote. What it does not explain is why any of it followed from the rest.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second account starts with an effect and works backward. San Francisco grew from about a thousand people to twenty-five thousand in two years, and the text asks what made that happen.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It then lays out the chain: a discovery, a newspaper story, cheap passage around Cape Horn, and a port that was the only place to land. Each link is given a reason.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Together the two show something neither shows alone. The timeline gives a reader the order of events; the cause and effect account gives the reader why that order was not an accident.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two accounts of the California gold rush sit side by side. One is a timeline. One is a cause and effect chain. Both cover the same eight years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The timeline begins in January of 1848. Gold was found at a sawmill. Then the news reached the east. Then came the ships. Then statehood in 1850.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It is easy to follow. It is easy to quote. It does not explain why one thing led to the next.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second account starts with an effect. San Francisco grew from a thousand people to twenty-five thousand in two years. The text asks what made that happen.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then it lays out the chain. A discovery. A newspaper story. Cheap passage around Cape Horn. A port that was the only place to land.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Together they show more than either one alone. The timeline gives the order. The other gives the reasons.

questions.q: What does the timeline leave out?
questions.a: It gives the order of events but does not explain why any of it followed from the rest.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the timeline) and paragraph E (i.e. the chain of causes).
Summarize how the two accounts of the gold rush are organized.
questions.a: One is a timeline running from the discovery at the sawmill in 1848 forward to statehood in 1850. The other starts with San Francisco's growth and works backward through a chain of causes: the discovery, the newspaper story, cheap passage and a single port.

questions.q:
timeline: an account that lists events in the order they happened.
passage: a journey by ship, or the fare paid for it.
Describe the connection between the growth of San Francisco and the chain of causes the second text gives.
questions.a: The second account begins with San Francisco growing from about a thousand people to twenty-five thousand in two years, then explains it through the discovery, the newspaper story, cheap passage around Cape Horn and a port that was the only place to land.

note: Have students draw both shapes before writing: an arrow for the timeline, a chain of boxes for the causes. The drawing usually makes the comparison easy.

title: Two Texts: Plastic in the Ocean
standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the overall structure of events, ideas, concepts, or information in two or more texts.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A research summary and a campaign leaflet both describe plastic in the ocean. The numbers in them match. The shape of the two documents does not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The research summary is organized by category. One section covers where the plastic comes from, one covers where it ends up, one covers what it does to animals, and one covers what is still unknown.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That structure makes the gaps visible. A reader can see that estimates of the total amount vary widely, because the text gives a whole section to what nobody has measured.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The leaflet is problem and solution, and it is much shorter. It states the problem in two sentences and then gives five things a reader can do this week.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Its structure hides the uncertainty on purpose. A leaflet that spent half its space on what is unknown would not move anybody to act, so the doubt is left out.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Both are honest about their facts, and they are built for different work. A reader who wants to know what is settled should not take the leaflet, and a reader who wants to act should not wait for the summary.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A research summary and a campaign leaflet both describe plastic in the ocean. The numbers match. The shape of the two documents does not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The research summary is sorted by category. One part covers where the plastic comes from. One covers where it ends up. One covers what it does to animals. One covers what is still unknown.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That structure makes the gaps easy to see. Estimates of the total amount vary widely. A whole section says so.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The leaflet is problem and solution. It is much shorter. It states the problem in two sentences. Then it lists five things a reader can do.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Its structure hides the doubt on purpose. A leaflet full of what is unknown would not move anyone to act.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Both are honest about their facts. They are built for different work. One tells you what is settled. One asks you to act.

questions.q: Why does the leaflet leave out what is unknown?
questions.a: A leaflet that spent half its space on what is unknown would not move anybody to act, so the doubt is left out on purpose.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. categories) and paragraph D (i.e. problem and solution).
Summarize how the two documents are built differently.
questions.a: The research summary is organized by category, with sections on where plastic comes from, where it ends up, what it does to animals and what is unknown. The leaflet is problem and solution: two sentences of problem and five things a reader can do this week.

questions.q:
category: a group that things are sorted into.
estimate: a careful guess at an amount that has not been measured exactly.
Describe the connection between the structure of a text and the job it is meant to do.
questions.a: The summary gives a whole section to what nobody has measured because its job is to show what is settled, and the leaflet states the problem in two sentences because its job is to get a reader to act this week.

note: Paragraph F keeps this from becoming a lesson about one text being dishonest. Both are accurate; they are built for different readers.

title: Two Texts: The Great Migration
standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the overall structure of events, ideas, concepts, or information in two or more texts.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Between 1916 and 1970, about six million Black Americans left the South for cities in the North and West. Two texts about that movement take almost opposite shapes.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is a statistical overview. It gives decade by decade figures: how many people left, which states they left, which cities they reached, and how the populations of Chicago and Detroit changed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its structure is comparison. Column against column, the text sets the South beside the North and one decade beside the next, so the size of the movement is impossible to miss.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second text follows one family from Mississippi to Chicago in 1937. It is a narrative, in time order, and it covers four days of a journey rather than fifty years of one.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What the narrative gives is the reason a column of numbers cannot. It shows a wage, a train car, a landlord, and a decision made at a kitchen table.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A reader who has both can do something neither text alone allows: place one family inside six million people, and recognize the six million as that many separate kitchen tables.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Between 1916 and 1970, about six million Black Americans left the South. They moved to cities in the North and West. Two texts about it take opposite shapes.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is an overview of numbers. It gives figures by decade. How many left. Which states. Which cities. How Chicago and Detroit changed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its structure is comparison. It sets the South beside the North. It sets one decade beside the next. The size is impossible to miss.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second text follows one family from Mississippi to Chicago in 1937. It is a narrative in time order. It covers four days, not fifty years.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The narrative gives what numbers cannot. It shows a wage, a train car, a landlord, and a choice made at a kitchen table.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A reader with both can do more. One family can be placed inside six million people. And six million can be seen as that many kitchen tables.

questions.q: How many people left the South, and over what years?
questions.a: About six million Black Americans left the South between 1916 and 1970 for cities in the North and West.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. comparison) and paragraph D (i.e. narrative).
Summarize how the two texts about the Great Migration are structured.
questions.a: The first is a statistical overview built on comparison, setting the South beside the North and one decade beside the next. The second is a narrative in time order following one family from Mississippi to Chicago over four days in 1937.

questions.q:
narrative: an account that tells a story in the order it happened.
overview: a broad account that gives the whole picture rather than the detail.
Describe the connection between the numbers in the first text and the family in the second.
questions.a: The narrative shows a wage, a train car and a decision made at a kitchen table, which lets a reader place one family inside the six million people the overview counts.

note: The last sentence of paragraph F is the one to read aloud twice. It names what comparing two structures is actually for.

title: Two Texts: The Return of the Bald Eagle
standard_text:
Standard: Compare and contrast the overall structure of events, ideas, concepts, or information in two or more texts.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.3 relationships · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1963 there were about 417 nesting pairs of bald eagles in the lower forty-eight states. By 2019 there were more than seventy thousand. Two accounts explain that recovery in different shapes.

paras.label: B
paras.text: One is a cause and effect text. It begins with the pesticide DDT, explains how it thinned eggshells so that eggs broke under the weight of a sitting parent, and traces the collapse from there.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It then follows the effects of a single decision: DDT was banned in 1972, eggshells thickened again, and the number of nesting pairs began to climb within a decade.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The other account is a sequence of actions. It lists the protections in order, the 1940 eagle act, the 1972 ban, the 1973 endangered species listing and the 2007 delisting, with a date on each.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The sequence is better for a timeline on a wall. The cause and effect version is better for answering why the eagles recovered rather than simply when.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A careful reader uses the sequence to check the chain. If eggshells had thickened before the ban, the cause and effect account would be wrong, and the dates are what make that test possible.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. cause and effect) and paragraph D (i.e. the sequence of actions).

questions.a: One is cause and effect: DDT thinned eggshells, the ban in 1972 let them thicken, and nesting pairs climbed. The other is a sequence of protections with a date on each, from the 1940 eagle act to the 2007 delisting.

questions.q:
pesticide: a chemical used to kill insects.
sequence: things set out in the order they happened.

questions.a: The dates let a reader test the chain, because if eggshells had thickened before the ban in 1972 the cause and effect account would be wrong.

note: Paragraph F is the real skill: using one structure to check another. It is worth more class time than naming the structures.

title: Two Views of the Boston Massacre
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
