paras.label: A
paras.text: On the night of March 5th, 1770, British soldiers fired into a crowd on King Street in Boston. Five men died. Almost everything else about the event was disputed within a week.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Paul Revere's engraving, sold around the colonies within three weeks, shows a line of soldiers firing on command into an unarmed, orderly crowd. An officer stands behind them with his sword raised.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The engraving is not a record. The street is drawn wider than it was, the crowd is drawn calm, and the clubs and snowballs that witnesses described are nowhere in the picture.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Captain Preston's own account, written days later, describes a mob throwing ice and swinging sticks, a soldier knocked down, and shots fired without any order from him at all.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A third account came out of the trial. John Adams defended the soldiers, and the jury heard dozens of witnesses contradict each other about whether the word fire was ever spoken.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The point of view in each one can be read from who made it. Revere was selling a cause, Preston was facing a hanging, and the court was deciding guilt. None of them was simply describing.

title: Who Saw the Shape of DNA
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: The 1953 paper announcing the double helix is one page long and carries two names, James Watson and Francis Crick. The story of how the shape was found takes more names than that.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Rosalind Franklin, working at King's College London, made X-ray photographs of DNA fibers. One of them, labelled Photo 51, showed a cross pattern that a trained reader could use to measure the shape.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Watson was shown that photograph by a colleague of Franklin's, without her knowledge. He later wrote that the moment he saw it, his mouth fell open and his pulse began to race.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Accounts of what happened next differ sharply. Watson's book describes Franklin as an obstacle; Franklin's notebooks show she had already worked out that the molecule was a helix with the backbones outside.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The Nobel Prize went to Watson, Crick and Maurice Wilkins in 1962. Franklin had died of cancer four years earlier at thirty-seven, and the prize is not awarded after death.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Reading several accounts changes the answer to a simple question. Who discovered the structure of DNA has one name in a textbook, two on the paper, and at least four in the record.

title: Two Letters Home from the Trail
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent.

 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two letters written on the same wagon train in 1852 survive. They describe the same two weeks on the Platte River and leave a reader with two different journeys.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is from a man of twenty-six travelling to take up land. He writes about distance made each day, the condition of the oxen, and the price of flour at Fort Laramie.

paras.label: C
paras.text: His letter has almost nothing in it about people. The word company appears four times and always means the wagons, never the families inside them.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second letter is from a woman of thirty-one with three children. Hers counts the graves they pass, names two families who turned back, and describes washing clothes in a river at the end of a day of walking.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Both are accurate. The man was responsible for stock and supplies; the woman was responsible for children and for everything that happened once the wagons stopped.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A reader who has only one of them will get the trail wrong. Together they show that what a person notices on a journey depends on what that person is answerable for.

title: The Argument About Pluto
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Pluto was called a planet from its discovery in 1930 until a vote in 2006. Nothing about Pluto changed in those seventy-six years. What changed was what astronomers had found around it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: By 2005 telescopes had turned up hundreds of icy bodies beyond Neptune, and one of them, Eris, appeared to be larger than Pluto. Either the solar system had a tenth planet, or it had fewer than nine.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Astronomers chose a definition with three parts: a planet orbits the sun, is round under its own gravity, and has cleared other objects out of its orbital path.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Pluto fails the third test. It crosses Neptune's path and shares its region with thousands of other bodies, so it was reclassified as a dwarf planet.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Many planetary scientists objected, and still do. They argue the third rule describes where an object sits rather than what it is, and that by the same rule a planet moved into a crowded orbit would stop being one.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Both sides are reading the same facts. The disagreement is about what a word should mean, which is a different kind of argument from one about what is true.

title: The Same Flood in Two Newspapers
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A river rose over its banks on a Tuesday night and two papers covered it on Wednesday morning. Both front pages are accurate. They are not the same story.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The city paper leads with the count: homes flooded, roads closed, people in shelters, dollars of damage estimated by the county. Its first quotation is from the emergency manager.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The town weekly leads with one street. It names six families, says which of them had flooded before, and prints what a woman said while standing in her kitchen.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The city paper's readers mostly live elsewhere. They need to know how big this is and whether their own roads are open, so scale comes first and names come later.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The weekly's readers live on that street or two streets over. They already know how big it is. What they do not know is who needs help and where to take it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Comparing the two teaches something about every account a reader meets. Whose questions a writer is answering shapes what goes in the first paragraph and what never appears at all.

title: Three Sources on a Snowstorm
standard_text:
Standard: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or to solve a problem efficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.9 integrating sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A storm is forecast for Thursday and a family needs three different answers: whether school will close, whether the roads will be drivable at six in the morning, and how much snow to expect in total.

paras.label: B
paras.text: No single source answers all three. The weather service forecast gives amounts and timing but says nothing about any particular school district or road.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The district website or its text alert answers the school question and nothing else. It will usually not post until early morning, because the district is waiting on the same forecast.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The state transportation department runs the third source: a map of plow locations and road conditions updated through the night. It answers the driving question and ignores the other two.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Knowing which source holds which answer is the whole skill. A person who checks only the forecast will guess at the roads; a person who checks only the alert will not know what is coming after.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The order matters too. Read the forecast on Wednesday to plan, check the road map at five, and look for the district alert last, because it is the only one that cannot come early.

title: Checking a Photograph
standard_text:
Standard: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or to solve a problem efficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.9 integrating sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A photograph of a flooded street is shared a hundred thousand times with a caption naming a city and a date. Checking whether the caption is true takes about four minutes and three sources.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is a reverse image search. Upload the picture and a search engine will list every earlier page it appeared on, which often shows the same image carrying a different date.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is a map. Street view and satellite images let a reader compare buildings, signs and the shape of a corner against what the photograph shows.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is a weather record. Archived observations say whether that city had rain on that day, and a flood without rain anywhere in the record is worth doubting.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Any one source can mislead on its own. An image may be new even if a search finds nothing, and a street can change between a satellite pass and a storm.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Together they are strong. A photograph that appeared online two years earlier, shows a corner that does not match the city, and falls on a dry day is not what the caption says.

title: Finding a Bird's Name
standard_text:
Standard: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or to solve a problem efficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.9 integrating sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A brown bird with a streaked chest lands on a feeder and a child wants its name. There are about eight hundred bird species in North America, and dozens of them are brown with streaked chests.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A field guide narrows it by region first. Range maps at the back show which species occur where, and a guide used properly cuts eight hundred down to perhaps forty before any feather is examined.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then it narrows by shape. Bill thickness tells a reader whether a bird cracks seeds or probes for insects, which divides the forty again without needing any color at all.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A sound recording does work no picture can. Many look-alike species sound nothing alike, and an app that matches a recording to a library will often name a bird the eye cannot separate.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The third source is a local sightings list. Birders post what they have seen that week, and a species nobody has reported within a hundred miles is probably not the one at the feeder.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Used together the three take minutes. Used alone, any one of them can send a beginner to a species that has never occurred in the state.

title: Planning a Visit to a National Park
standard_text:

paras.label: A
paras.text: A family has two days at a national park in July and wants to see three particular places. Doing that well is a research problem, and the park publishes most of the answer in pieces.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The official park site holds the hours, the entrance fee, and the alerts. Alerts matter most: a road closed by rockfall in June will make a planned route impossible in July.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The campground reservation system is a separate source with its own calendar. Sites in popular parks open on a fixed date months ahead and are gone within minutes of opening.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Trail conditions come from a third place. Rangers post recent reports on snow, water crossings and insects, and a trail that is open on the map can still be impassable that week.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A fourth source is the weather forecast for the elevation, not for the nearest town. A trailhead four thousand feet higher than the town can be twenty degrees colder and under cloud.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Reading them in the right order saves the trip. Check alerts, then reservations, then conditions, then weather, because each one can make the next question pointless.

paras.text: The official park site holds the hours, the fee and the alerts. Alerts matter most. A road closed by rockfall will ruin a planned route.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The campground booking system is a separate source. It has its own calendar. Sites open months ahead and are gone within minutes.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Trail conditions come from a third place. Rangers post reports on snow, water and insects. An open trail can still be impassable.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A fourth source is the weather forecast for the elevation. A trailhead can be much colder than the town below it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Reading them in order saves the trip. Alerts, then reservations, then conditions, then weather. Each one can make the next question pointless.

questions.q: Why do alerts matter most on the park site?
questions.a: A road closed by rockfall in June will make a planned route impossible in July, so an alert can cancel a plan before anything else is decided.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. reservations) and paragraph E (i.e. weather at elevation).
Summarize the order a family should read the sources in.
questions.a: Check the park site's alerts first, then the campground reservation calendar, then the ranger reports on trail conditions, then the forecast for the elevation rather than the town, because each one can make the next question pointless.

questions.q:
alert: a notice warning of a change or a hazard.
elevation: how high a place is above sea level.
Describe the connection between the elevation of a trailhead and the forecast a family should read.
questions.a: A trailhead four thousand feet higher than the town can be twenty degrees colder and under cloud, so the forecast for the town is the wrong one to plan from.

note: Paragraph F is the transferable idea: sequence the sources so a dead end shows up before any work is wasted on it.

title: Reading a Nutrition Label
standard_text:
Standard: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or to solve a problem efficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.9 integrating sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two cereal boxes sit on a shelf and one claims to be healthier. Deciding whether that is true means reading three parts of the package rather than the front of it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The serving size at the top of the label governs every number below it. A cereal listing 110 calories per serving is not lower in calories if its serving is three quarters of a cup against the other's full cup.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The ingredient list is the second source. Ingredients appear in order of weight, so a product with sugar in the first three places contains more sugar than most of what else is in the box.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Sugar also travels under other names. Cane syrup, dextrose, fruit juice concentrate and honey are each listed separately, which can keep any one of them out of the first three places.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The third place to look is the percent daily value column. It converts an unfamiliar number of milligrams into a share of a day, which is far easier to compare between two boxes.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The front of the box is not a source. Words like natural and wholesome are not defined by any rule, and the claim a shopper can actually check is always on the back.

note: Bring two real boxes. Students who compare the serving sizes first find the trick without being told it is there.

title: The Case for Keeping the Old Bridge
standard_text:
Standard: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which point(s).
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension

paras.label: A
paras.text: A town council has to choose between repairing a ninety-year-old bridge and replacing it. A letter from the historical society argues for repair, and it is worth reading for how it argues.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Its first point is cost. The letter gives an engineer's estimate of four million dollars for repair against seven million for replacement, and cites the report by date and page.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Its second point is time. It claims a repair closes the bridge for eight months and a replacement for two years, and supports that with the schedule from a nearby town that replaced a similar span.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Its third point is character, and here the support is different. The letter offers photographs, a quotation from a resident, and the fact that the bridge appears on the town seal.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A careful reader sorts those. The first two points rest on numbers that could be checked and disputed; the third rests on what people value, which no report can settle.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The letter is stronger for keeping them separate. It does not pretend that liking the bridge is a cost figure, and it does not hide the cost figures behind a photograph.

Summarize the three points and the support for each.

estimate: a careful calculation of what something will cost.

note: RI.5.8 asks which evidence supports which point. A three-column chart with point, evidence and whether it could be checked does the work.

title: Why Not to Feed Ducks Bread
standard_text:
Standard: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which point(s).
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A park sign asks visitors not to feed bread to ducks. The sign gives three reasons, and the evidence behind them is not equally strong.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first reason is nutrition. Bread fills a duck without feeding it, and studies of waterfowl raised on a high-bread diet show deformed wing growth, a condition called angel wing.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That evidence is direct. Birds were raised under measured conditions and the result was recorded, so the claim and the study are about the same thing.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second reason is water quality. Uneaten bread decays, feeding bacteria and algae that lower the oxygen in a pond, which is supported by measurements taken at heavily fed ponds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The third reason is crowding. The sign says feeding draws more birds than a pond can support, which spreads disease. The support here is weaker: it rests on reasoning rather than on a count at that pond.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A reader who sorts the three is better placed than one who either believes all of them or dismisses the sign. Two reasons carry measurements; one carries an argument.

questions.q: What is angel wing, and what causes it?
questions.a: It is a deformed wing growth seen in waterfowl raised on a high-bread diet, because bread fills a duck without feeding it.

questions.a: Nutrition is supported by studies of birds raised on bread that developed angel wing. Water quality is supported by measurements at heavily fed ponds. Crowding is supported only by reasoning, not by a count at that pond.

Describe the connection between uneaten bread and the oxygen in a pond.
questions.a: Uneaten bread decays and feeds bacteria and algae, and those lower the oxygen in the pond, which is supported by measurements taken at heavily fed ponds.

note: Weaker support is not the same as wrong. Paragraph E says the reasoning may well be right; it says nobody counted at that pond.

title: The Argument for a Crosswalk
standard_text:
Standard: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which point(s).
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Students at a middle school asked their city council for a crosswalk outside the front gate. Their presentation is a clean example of matching each kind of evidence to the claim it is meant to support.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Their first claim was that people already cross there. The support was a tally: two students counted crossings for five mornings and recorded 412 of them, with the sheets attached.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Their second claim was that the crossing is dangerous. Here they used the city's own crash records, which listed two collisions and one injury at that corner in four years.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Their third claim was that a crosswalk would help. That one needed outside evidence, so they cited a transportation study of marked crossings with a pedestrian island.

paras.label: E
paras.text: They also named what they could not show. Nobody could prove a future collision would be prevented, and the presentation said so rather than overstating the study.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The council approved the crosswalk. The tally mattered most, because it was the only piece of evidence nobody in the room could dispute: the students had gone out and counted it themselves.

note: Paragraph E is the part to praise. Naming the limit of your own evidence makes the rest of it more believable, not less.

title: Should the School Put Solar Panels on the Roof?
standard_text:
Standard: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which point(s).
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A school board received two reports on putting solar panels on the gym roof. Both were written by engineers, both used real numbers, and the two reached opposite recommendations.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first report supports the panels. Its central evidence is a twenty-five year total: the system costs $340,000 and would save about $620,000 in electricity over its life.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second report opposes them. Its central evidence is the roof itself, which has eleven years left before replacement, and removing and reinstalling panels would cost $45,000.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Neither report is hiding anything. They disagree because they chose different time spans, and a twenty-five year argument and an eleven year argument can both be true at once.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The board found the question underneath the disagreement. It was not whether solar panels save money, but whether to replace the roof first, and neither report had been asked to answer that.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is what reading for reasons and evidence is for. The strongest move a reader can make is noticing which question the evidence was gathered to answer.

questions.q:
recommendation: the course of action a report advises.
span: a stretch of time from one point to another.
Describe the connection between the time span a report uses and the recommendation it reaches.
questions.a: A twenty-five year span makes the electricity savings of about $620,000 decisive, while an eleven year span makes the $45,000 cost of removing and reinstalling the panels decisive, so the same numbers support opposite recommendations.

note: This is the hardest of the five and the most useful. Two honest reports, no villain, and the disagreement sitting in the question rather than the data.

title: Naming the Park
standard_text:
Standard: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which point(s).
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.6 point of view · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A city asked residents to propose a name for a new park, then published the three finalists with the case made for each. The three cases are not built the same way.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first proposes the name of a teacher who ran a free summer program on that land for thirty years. The case rests on testimony: eleven letters from former students, quoted at length.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second proposes a name from the language of the people who lived there first, and that case rests on documents, a treaty map and a historical society's record of the place name.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third proposes naming it after the creek that runs through it. The case is practical: the name is already in use, appears on maps, and would need no explanation to anyone.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Each case is strong for a different reason. Testimony shows what a place has meant, documents show what it was called, and practicality shows what will actually be said out loud.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The council will have to decide which reason counts most, and no amount of further evidence will settle that. Choosing between good reasons is a different task from weighing evidence.

title: Three Texts on the Monarch Butterfly
standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A student writing about monarch butterflies has three texts on the desk: a life cycle diagram, a tagging study, and a news article about milkweed. None of them is the report, and together they are.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The diagram gives the sequence. Egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, adult, and the detail that an adult born in late summer lives eight months while one born in June lives about five weeks.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The tagging study gives the distance. Volunteers put numbered stickers on wings in Canada and the tags turned up in Mexico, which is how the three-thousand-mile migration was first proved.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The news article gives the problem. Milkweed is the only plant monarch caterpillars eat, and it has been cleared from most farm edges in the midwest over the last thirty years.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Put together they answer a question none of them asks. The long-lived late-summer generation is the one that makes the whole journey, and it needs milkweed at both ends of a route it has never flown.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That is what integrating sources means. The student is not summarizing three texts in turn but using them to say something none of their authors wrote down.

note: Paragraph F names the standard. A student who writes three paragraphs, one per source, has summarized rather than integrated.

title: Three Texts on the Cliff Houses
standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Three sources describe the stone houses built into the cliffs of the Colorado Plateau, and a reader who uses only one will come away with a picture that is partly wrong.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is an archaeological report. It dates the main building period to the twelve hundreds, counts the rooms at Cliff Palace at about 150, and notes that the sites were occupied for less than a century.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is a tree-ring record. Beams cut from the roofs can be dated to the year, and the rings show a severe drought across the region in the eleven seventies and again in the twelve seventies.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third comes from Pueblo people today. Hopi and Zuni accounts describe the cliff sites not as a place that was abandoned but as one stop on a long migration that continued south.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A reader who has only the report thinks of an unsolved mystery. One who has only the tree rings thinks drought drove everyone out. One who has only the Pueblo accounts misses the dates.

paras.label: F
paras.text: All three together give something steadier: a hard climate, a decision to move, and descendants who never stopped describing the move as something their ancestors chose to do.

title: Three Texts on Hibernation
standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Hibernation sounds like one thing and is not. Three sources about three animals show that the word covers several different strategies for getting through a winter.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A ground squirrel account describes true hibernation. Body temperature falls to near freezing, the heart slows to a few beats a minute, and the animal wakes only every week or two to shiver warm again.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A bear account describes something else. A denning bear's temperature drops only a few degrees, it does not eat or drink for months, and it can wake and move within a minute if disturbed.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A frog account is stranger than either. Some wood frogs freeze solid, with ice between their cells and sugar packed inside them to keep the cells from bursting, and thaw in spring.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Reading only one gives a wrong rule. A student who learns the bear case will say hibernating animals wake easily; one who learns the squirrel case will say they cannot be roused at all.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Taken together the three give a better definition. Hibernation is any way of surviving a season on stored resources, and what the body does depends on how big it is and how cold it gets.

title: Three Texts on the Chicago Fire
standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: The fire that burned Chicago in October of 1871 destroyed about three and a half square miles of the city. Three kinds of source describe it, and they are useful for different things.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first is the fire department's own inquiry. It records the alarm raised at about nine on a Sunday evening, a wrong box pulled, and an engine sent to the wrong street for over an hour.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second is the set of newspaper accounts printed in the weeks after. They are vivid, and they are also where the story about a cow kicking over a lantern first appeared, which a reporter later admitted he had invented.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The third is the insurance record. Claims filed after the fire describe building materials street by street, and they show how much of the burned district was wooden, including the sidewalks.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Each has a weakness. The inquiry was written by people whose work was being judged, the newspapers were competing for readers, and the insurance claims covered only what was insured.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Used together they answer the real question. The fire spread as it did because of a dry autumn, a wooden city, and an hour lost at the start, and no cow was required.

title: Three Texts on Antarctic Ice
standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
 Spiral: RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.5 structure · RI.5.7 multiple sources · RI.5.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Three sources describe the ice of Antarctica, and a reader who mixes them up will reach a conclusion that none of them supports.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The first measures sea ice: frozen ocean water that forms each winter and melts each summer, covering an area larger than the continent at its peak and nearly vanishing by February.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second measures the ice sheet: fresh water locked on land, in places more than two miles thick, built up over hundreds of thousands of years of snowfall.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The two behave differently and matter differently. Melting sea ice does not raise sea level, because the ice is already floating; melting land ice does, because it adds water that was not in the ocean.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The third source is a satellite record of mass. Since 2002 a pair of satellites has weighed the continent by measuring tiny changes in gravity, and the land ice has been losing mass.

paras.label: F
paras.text: A headline about record ice can be true of the sea ice in the same year the ice sheet is shrinking. Knowing which ice a sentence is about is the difference between reading the news and misreading it.

note: A glass of water with an ice cube in it settles paragraph D in thirty seconds. Mark the level, let it melt, look again.

title: The Mail That Went by Mule
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 4-5 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Until 2023 the United States ran one mail route that no vehicle could reach. Letters and parcels for the village of Supai, at the bottom of a side canyon of the Grand Canyon, went down on mules.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The village sits eight miles from the nearest road, down a trail that drops two thousand feet through switchbacks too narrow and too steep for a truck of any size.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A train of mules left the canyon rim most mornings carrying sorted mail in canvas panniers. Each animal took about a hundred and thirty pounds, and the trip down ran three to five hours.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Everything the village used came the same way. Groceries, building supplies, mattresses and school books were all weighed, balanced in pairs so the two loads matched, and roped on.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The mail was stamped with a special postmark, and the route was the last official pack-mule mail service in the country. Helicopters now carry much of the load.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The route lasted because the alternative was worse. Building a road would have cut through the canyon the village lives in, and for more than a century mules were simply the sensible answer.

title: The Clock in Your Body
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 4-5 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: Almost every cell in the human body keeps time. A small group of neurons behind the eyes sets the pace, and the rhythm it runs on is close to twenty-four hours but not exactly.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Light is what corrects it. Special cells in the retina, separate from those used for seeing, report brightness to that clock and shift it forward or back by a few minutes each day.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The shifting explains jet lag. Flown across six time zones, a traveller's clock is six hours out and moves at roughly an hour a day, which is why the body takes most of a week to agree with the local one.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The clock controls more than sleep. Body temperature, blood pressure, hunger and the release of several hormones all follow it, and some medicines work measurably better at particular hours.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Adolescence shifts the whole rhythm later. Through the teenage years the clock runs behind a child's or an adult's by one to three hours, which is a change in biology rather than a habit.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That shift is why school start times are argued about. A teenager told to sleep at nine is being asked to do something their clock is not yet releasing them to do.

title: The Woman Who Finished the Bridge
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 4-5 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Brooklyn Bridge was designed by John Roebling, who died of tetanus before construction began. His son Washington took over, and within three years he could not leave his room.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The cause was the work underwater. Men dug in sealed chambers called caissons, under pressure, and rising too quickly left them with crippling pain that nobody yet knew how to prevent.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Washington was left partly paralysed and unable to speak above a whisper. The bridge had eleven years left to build and a chief engineer who could not go to the site.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Emily Roebling, his wife, became the link. She learned cable construction, stress analysis and the mathematics of catenary curves, and carried instructions and answers between her husband and the site every day.

paras.label: E
paras.text: For more than a decade she met the contractors and the trustees. When politicians moved to replace Washington, she argued the case for keeping him and the board voted with her.

paras.label: F
paras.text: She was the first person to ride across the finished bridge in 1883, carrying a rooster for luck. A plaque on the bridge names all three Roeblings, which is the honest version of the story.

title: The Channel That Carries Whale Song
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 4-5 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: A fin whale's call can be detected by a listening station a thousand miles away. The reason is not the loudness of the whale alone but a layer of the ocean that behaves like a pipe.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Sound in water bends toward whatever slows it down. Speed falls as water gets colder and rises as pressure increases, so between the cold surface layers and the deep high-pressure water there is a depth where sound travels slowest.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Sound that enters that depth cannot easily leave. A wave angling upward bends back down, a wave angling downward bends back up, and the energy is trapped in a horizontal channel instead of spreading in all directions.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The layer sits around half a mile down in most oceans and is called the SOFAR channel. It was discovered in the nineteen forties, when researchers set off small charges and heard them hours later across an ocean basin.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Several baleen whales call at frequencies that suit it, low and long, below the range of most human hearing. Blue and fin whale calls are among the loudest sounds any animal makes.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Shipping noise sits in the same frequencies and the same channel. Recordings show whales raising the pitch and loudness of their calls where traffic is heavy, and the range a call carries has shrunk.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A fin whale's call can be heard a thousand miles away. The reason is not only the whale. A layer of the ocean acts like a pipe.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Sound in water bends toward whatever slows it down. Cold water slows it. High pressure speeds it. So there is a depth where sound is slowest.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Sound that enters that depth cannot leave easily. A wave angling up bends back down. A wave angling down bends back up. The energy stays in a channel.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The layer sits about half a mile down. It is called the SOFAR channel. It was found in the nineteen forties.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Several whales call at low frequencies that suit it. Blue and fin whale calls are among the loudest sounds any animal makes.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Shipping noise sits in the same channel. Where traffic is heavy, whales raise the pitch and loudness of their calls. The range a call carries has shrunk.

questions.q: Why can a whale call travel a thousand miles?
questions.a: Sound that enters the depth where it travels slowest is trapped in a horizontal channel, because a wave angling upward bends back down and a wave angling downward bends back up.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the trapping) and paragraph F (i.e. shipping noise).
Summarize how the SOFAR channel works.
questions.a: Sound in water bends toward whatever slows it down, and about half a mile deep the cold and the pressure balance so sound travels slowest there. Sound entering that depth bends back into it instead of spreading, so it carries horizontally for a thousand miles.

questions.q:
frequency: how high or low a sound is.
channel: a path that keeps something travelling in one direction.
Describe the connection between shipping noise and whale calls.
questions.a: Shipping noise sits in the same frequencies and the same channel, so where traffic is heavy whales raise the pitch and loudness of their calls and the range a call carries has shrunk.

note: This is the densest article in the grade 5 set, which is what RI.5.10 asks for. Read paragraph B twice before going on.

title: The Code Talkers
standard_text:
Standard: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 4-5 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
 Spiral: RI.5.1 quoting · RI.5.2 main ideas · RI.5.4 word meaning · RI.5.8 reasons and evidence
 Lower range: LL 690 – 790

paras.label: A
paras.text: During the Second World War, American forces in the Pacific needed a way to send orders by radio that the other side could not read. Machine codes existed, but encoding and decoding a message took half an hour.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The answer was a language rather than a cipher. Navajo was spoken by fewer than thirty people outside the Navajo Nation, had no written form in wide use, and was unrelated to any European or Asian language.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Around four hundred Navajo marines served as code talkers. They did not simply speak Navajo: they built a code inside it, with Navajo words standing for letters and for military terms.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A submarine became an iron fish, a dive bomber a chicken hawk, and a general a war chief. A message that took half an hour on a machine took about twenty seconds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The code was never broken. It stayed classified until 1968, which meant the men who built it could not explain what they had done for more than twenty years after the war.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Many of them had been punished as children for speaking Navajo in government boarding schools. The language those schools tried to end became one the United States military could not do without.
